scope: Selected primary menswear sources, not all designers or a universal scientific style law.

sources.title: The Art of the Shirt and Tie Combo
sources.supported: Choose a focal garment; consider tonal, adjacent and complementary palettes; usually deeper ties with lighter shirts; vary pattern scale and assess visible weave texture. It explicitly pairs lilac with purple/deep-pink paisley.
sources.limit: Its lighter-tie advice is written as an absolute. This implementation treats it as a workwear preference, not a universal prohibition. No numerical coefficients are supplied by the source.

sources.title: How to combine your suit and shoe colors
sources.supported: Choose footwear according to dress level, suit/trouser colour and depth. Navy can use black, navy or cognac. Grey can use black or brown of appropriate depth. Very dark brown/deep red can be used with black; light blue can use black or navy.
sources.limit: Supports contextual choice, not a cognac ban or black-only rule. Does not rank the owner's specific shoes or supply price/brand bonuses.

sources.title: Suit, shirt and tie combinations
sources.supported: Examples include navy with white/sky-blue and burgundy/blue/brown ties, and brown with beige/white and a different-depth brown tie; pattern sizes should differ.
sources.limit: Other portions are restrictive about mixed geometric patterns and give skin-tone generalizations. Those are not adopted as hard bans or demographic rules. No source-provided numerical scales.

sources.publisher: Boggi Milano Egypt / regional retail site
sources.title: Ties and Bow Ties — styling FAQ
sources.supported: Tie should be readable against the shirt; a deeper tie is its general formal guideline. Gives navy/charcoal/mid-grey/brown tie directions and distinguishes plain, stripe, micro-pattern and knit styles.
sources.limit: Its warning against navy disappearing into navy is not an unconditional navy-on-navy ban; compare CT's tonal approach. The module uses bounded readability guidance, not this source as a universal authority.

sources.title: Richmond 2 Black & Ocean Suede
sources.supported: Maker describes this specific suede loafer with black, grey or navy tailoring and even dinner wear. This disproves a blanket statement that suede can never accompany tailoring.
sources.limit: Product-specific example, not a rule that every suede shoe is formal or that the user owns this shoe. No product was added to the wardrobe.

sources.title: Men's mix and match suits
sources.supported: Odd jacket/trousers should look deliberately coordinated rather than almost matching accidentally; examples include navy with grey/beige. Keep fabric-weight compatibility in view.
sources.limit: Calendar tags alone do not establish fibre weight; the earlier seasonal-veto defect is not restored. Its strict colour-count language is not adopted literally for small pattern accents.

rules.implementation: Readable shirt/tie hierarchy; generally deeper tie. Penalize muddled or reverse-value work combinations softly, without maximizing jacket-shirt contrast.
Relative scale, prominence and leading/supporting pattern; compound checks remain compound, quiet textures remain quiet.
Tonal/adjacent/coordinated accents; distinct lavender, warm-neutral and brown depths; contextual shirt/tie family directions.
Evaluate separate trousers against blazer shade/depth rather than simulate a mismatched suit.
Footwear context includes trouser depth, dress level, material and conspicuous decoration. Neither cognac nor suede is universally prohibited.
Whole-outfit focus and coherency; shoe/watch context. No brand, price or status reward.
10% of clothing estimate compares property patterns to the two previously preferred independent sets. No exact-ID reward, inferred per-outfit approval, fitted model or invented source score.
rules.kind: owner-context-inspired semantic prior, not web fact

rules.implementation: Two uses maximum per unanchored physical item; exact anchor exempts only itself. No Tie at most two unless selected. No duplicate clothing padding.
